h1: Outdoor living, from the terrace to the roofline
hero_sub: Covered terraces, summer kitchens, pool decks, pergolas, driveways, stucco and impact openings across Miami-Dade and Broward. Engineered for High-Velocity Hurricane Zone loads, permitted and inspected, and built under the license of an insured general contractor with 20-plus years in this market.
local_heading: Built for weather that tests everything
intro_paragraphs: At the high end in South Florida, outdoor living is not a grill on a slab and a string of cafe lights. It is a covered room with a finished ceiling, a summer kitchen with permitted gas and water, a pool deck in travertine or large-format porcelain, and openings that let the house and the yard behave like one space. The people who build it are not entertaining twice a year. They are outside most evenings from October through June, and they want the outside of the house detailed to the same standard as the kitchen inside it.

Miami-Dade and Broward are the only two counties in Florida's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, so anything that spans, shades or opens has to be engineered and built from approved products: a Miami-Dade Notice of Acceptance, or a state approval that covers the HVHZ, with large-missile and cyclic pressure testing behind it. Each county layers its own amendments onto the Florida Building Code through a Board of Rules and Appeals that certifies building officials countywide. Near the water, salt air decides which hardware survives a decade. In a flood zone, elevation and the substantial-improvement rule decide what can be built at all. In a condo, the association reviews before the city does.

Every project starts with a site walk and ends as a fixed written scope: what gets demolished, what goes under the slab, how the deck drains, which products carry which approvals, and what the finished thing is made of. We pull the permits under Lic. CGC1539072 and sequence the work the way it actually has to happen: footings and underground utilities first, then structure, then waterproofing, then the finishes nobody wants to see torn up twice. Trade rough-ins are inspected before they are buried. A supervisor is on site daily. The permit is closed at final inspection, which is the only version of done that shows up in county records.

The work changes with the address. In Coral Gables and Miami Beach, the design review board sees it before the building department does. On Key Biscayne, Golden Beach and Fisher Island it answers to salt. Along the Fort Lauderdale waterfront, in Coral Ridge, Rio Vista, Harbor Beach and the Las Olas isles, the yard runs to a seawall and the dock is part of the plan. Out west in Weston, Parkland, Southwest Ranches and Plantation Acres it is an acre, an association, and a screen enclosure with a decision to make. We build all of it across 42 areas in both counties, with 150-plus remodels and additions behind us. Pick yours below.
scope_intro: Exterior work is one project or it is five arguments. These are the pieces we design, permit, build and warrant as a single coordinated scope.

scope_items.name: Covered terraces and loggias
scope_items.desc: Roofed outdoor rooms tied into the existing structure with engineered connections, finished ceilings, concealed lighting and drainage that treats the terrace as part of the house rather than an afterthought.

scope_items.name: Summer kitchens with real utilities
scope_items.desc: Gas, water and power run under permit to cabinetry rated for the weather, sealed stone counters and marine-grade stainless, so year five still looks like the day it was finished.

scope_items.name: Pool decks, driveways and hardscape
scope_items.desc: Travertine, coral stone, large-format porcelain and pavers laid on a base built to drain, sloped away from the sliders, with the under-slab work priced instead of assumed.

scope_items.name: Pergolas engineered for uplift
scope_items.desc: Shade structures with signed and sealed engineering, footings sized for the load and connections detailed for hurricane uplift, proportioned to the house instead of to the widest available span.

scope_items.name: Impact doors and exterior openings
scope_items.desc: Sliding and folding walls, terrace doors and windows in HVHZ-approved units, installed with the bucks, anchors and spacing the product approval actually calls for.

scope_items.name: Exterior finishes and re-roof timing
scope_items.desc: Facade restoration, stucco repair and color changes cleared through review, with roofing scheduled alongside the exterior work so the property is torn up once instead of twice.

faqs.q: How much does a covered terrace and summer kitchen run?
faqs.a: It is driven by structure and utilities first, selections second. A new paver or travertine deck is one order of magnitude. A roofed outdoor room with engineered footings, permitted gas, water and power, a finished ceiling and a full summer kitchen is another one entirely. Appliances, stone and impact openings then move it again. Our number comes off a site walk and a written specification that names the drainage and everything under the slab, so you are comparing a real scope instead of a square-foot figure that quietly leaves out the expensive half.

faqs.q: What is a realistic timeline for the exterior?
faqs.a: Design, engineering and permitting usually take longer than the building does, and that is the part most homeowners underestimate. A deck replacement is measured in weeks on site. A covered outdoor room with utilities, a new roof structure and impact openings runs in months, with the permit and approval stage ahead of it. Weather and inspection sequencing set the rest of the pace. We give you a schedule tied to the scope, and we tell you which dates are ours and which belong to a building department.

faqs.q: Do a pergola, a patio or a summer kitchen really need permits?
faqs.a: Yes. In Miami-Dade and Broward, structures need a building permit and signed, sealed engineering for wind load; the gas, water and electrical serving an outdoor kitchen need their own trade permits and rough-in inspections; and pool decks, driveways and pool safety barriers require permits too. Building it quietly does not save you anything: unpermitted exterior work turns up in an appraisal, an insurance inspection or a title search, and it is far more expensive to legalize afterward than to file correctly the first time.

faqs.q: What keeps an exterior project from breaking ground?
faqs.a: A short list, and none of it is the building itself. A protected tree standing where the terrace wants to go, which needs its own permit and sometimes mitigation. An association or design review board that has not seen the material samples yet. A flood zone, where elevation and the substantial-improvement rule can reshape the design. And an incomplete submittal, usually missing engineering or a product approval that does not cover the HVHZ. All four are avoidable. All four are why we do the paperwork before the demolition.

faqs.q: Who is working in my yard, and under whose license?
faqs.a: PGX crews and PGX subcontractors, under a supervisor who is on site daily and reachable by name. We are the licensed general contractor of record under Lic. CGC1539072, which means the permits, the inspections, the trade coordination and the mess are ours, not yours. You get one point of contact from the first walk-through to the warranty, and in gated and estate communities our crews work to the hours, access and conduct rules the association enforces, because a quiet, tidy job site is part of the job.

faqs.q: How close to the water before salt air becomes a material problem?
faqs.a: Closer than most people expect, and it is chlorides that do the damage. Ordinary 304 stainless pits and streaks within a few years of steady salt exposure; 316 contains molybdenum and holds up far longer in the same spot. The same logic governs fasteners, hinges, appliance housings, light fixtures, cable railings and the sealer on your stone. On a bayfront or oceanfront lot we specify for the exposure up front, because replacing a rusted outdoor kitchen costs more than specifying it correctly did.
